introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2022. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

Each question carries twenty-five marks. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Discuss any **TWO** processes of soil formation.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Soil formation (pedogenesis)** results from the interaction of parent material, climate, relief, organisms and time. Two of the processes are discussed (3 marks each); the others are in the note at the end.

**1. Weathering of the parent material.** Rock is broken down in place by physical weathering (heating and cooling, frost action, salt crystallisation), chemical weathering (hydrolysis, oxidation, carbonation, solution) and biological weathering (roots and burrowing animals). This creates the loose mineral material (regolith) that supplies clay, sand and silt and the plant nutrients. In the humid tropics, chemical weathering is the fastest because of heat and moisture, so soils can be several metres deep.

**2. Leaching and ferralitisation (laterisation).** In hot, wet areas, heavy rain percolates through the regolith and dissolves and carries downwards (leaching) the soluble bases (calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium) and silica. What remains in the upper horizons are the insoluble **iron and aluminium oxides**, which give the typical deep red or yellow colour. The result is a deep, acid, nutrient-poor ferralitic soil, with a thin humus layer because litter decomposes fast. This is the process at work in the soils of the rainforest in southern Cameroon.

*Other processes that could be chosen:* **humification** (the decay of litter into humus, which darkens the topsoil and binds particles); **podzolisation** (leaching of iron and aluminium by acid humus in cool, wet coniferous areas, giving a bleached layer); **calcification** (upward movement of calcium carbonate in dry grasslands); **gleying** (waterlogging, which turns iron compounds grey-blue); **salinisation** (salts left behind by evaporation in dry areas); and the mixing of soil by earthworms and termites.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) i) Account for the variations in the relative sizes of nutrient stores of the tropical rainforest biome.

(7 marks)

ii) Briefly explain how **TWO** named human activities have destabilized a named ecosystem in the tropics.

(6 marks)

iii) What **TWO** measures can be adopted to curb the destruction of ecosystem balance?

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Variation in the relative sizes of nutrient stores in the tropical rainforest biome (7 marks)**

The nutrient cycle is shown by the Gersmehl model, in which the circles represent the three stores (biomass, litter, soil) and the arrows the flows between them.

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2022-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_1.png)

- **Biomass is by far the largest store.** Constant heat, moisture and sunlight give a very high productivity: the forest is dense, tall and multi-layered, and the trees take up nutrients continuously, so most of the nutrients of the ecosystem are held in the living vegetation.
- **Litter is the smallest store.** Leaves fall all the year, but the warm, moist conditions allow bacteria, fungi and termites to decompose the litter within weeks, so little accumulates on the floor. The flow of nutrients from litter to soil and back into the plants is rapid.
- **The soil store is small.** The deeply weathered ferralitic soil is acid and has been leached by very heavy rain; the clay holds few nutrients, and any nutrients released by decay are taken up at once by the shallow, dense root mat (often helped by mycorrhizal fungi) before the rain can wash them away. Inputs from rain and rock weathering and losses by leaching are both small.
- **Conclusion:** the nutrients are held in the vegetation and recycled quickly (a closed, fast cycle), not stored in the soil. When the forest is cleared, the biomass store is lost and the soil cannot replace it, which explains why cleared forest land quickly loses its fertility.

**(ii) How two named human activities have destabilised a named ecosystem in the tropics (6 marks)**

*Named ecosystem:* the **tropical rainforest of the Congo Basin in southern and eastern Cameroon**.

1. **Commercial logging.** Selective logging removes the best trees and the roads and skidding tracks open the canopy and compact the soil. The nutrients locked up in the timber are exported, the microclimate becomes hotter and drier, the soil is exposed to rain and is eroded and leached, and animals lose habitat. Cameroon is a major exporter of tropical timber, and the roads built for logging open the forest to hunters and farmers.
2. **Clearing for agriculture (shifting cultivation, cash crops and plantations).** Forest is cut and burnt for food crops, cocoa farms and large oil palm and rubber plantations. This replaces a diverse ecosystem by a few species, the nutrient cycle is broken, the soil becomes infertile and eroded within a few years, biodiversity is lost and carbon dioxide is released.

(Alternative activities: mining, hunting and the bushmeat trade, dam construction and urban expansion. In the Amazon, cattle ranching is the main activity.)

**(iii) Two measures to curb the destruction of ecosystem balance (6 marks)**

1. **Protected areas and the enforcement of conservation laws.** National parks and reserves, such as Korup National Park, the Dja Faunal Reserve (a World Heritage Site) and Campo Ma'an National Park in Cameroon, keep large areas of forest free from logging and farming, protect the biodiversity and allow wildlife to survive; they must be supported by anti-poaching patrols, fines for illegal logging and the participation of local communities, which also need an alternative income (ecotourism, community forestry).
2. **Sustainable forest management and reforestation.** Selective, controlled logging with felling quotas and rotation, a ban on exporting raw logs, certification of timber (for example by the Forest Stewardship Council), replanting of felled areas and agroforestry (growing crops under trees) allow people to use the forest while keeping its cover and its nutrient cycle. International schemes such as REDD+ pay countries to reduce deforestation.

(Other measures: education of the public, the use of fuel-efficient stoves and alternative energy to cut firewood, and the intensification of farming on existing land.)
